subject: Geography
board: National Curriculum (KS1-3), aligned to AQA GCSE 9-1
source: National Curriculum (KS1 geography: continents and oceans, hot and cold places, atlas and compass skills) | Spring 2 2027: TGA Year 2 pack, Topic, Towers, Tunnels & Turrets (towers around the world) | Summer 1 2027 (lessons 6 to 8): TGA Year 2 pack, Topic, Street Detectives; fieldwork from the door or window with an adult

lessons.title: The seven continents
objectives: Find each continent on a world map or globe
Say which continent is the biggest

keywords.def: one of the seven very large areas of land on Earth
a ball-shaped model of the Earth
a flat picture of the whole Earth
the biggest continent on Earth

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four countries of the UK.
What do we call a drawing of a place from above?
What is the name of the country where we live?

teach.heading: Our big planet
bullets: We live on planet Earth.
Earth has land and water.
The big areas of land are called continents.
teach.note: Hold up a globe or show one on screen and turn it slowly. Ask: what colours can you see? Blue is water and other colours are land. Say that Allah created the Earth with land and sea. Explain that a continent is a very big piece of land, much larger than a country.

teach.heading: Seven continents
bullets: Asia, Africa, North America and South America.
Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
There are seven continents in all.
teach.note: Use a chant to learn the names: tap out the number of seven on your fingers. Show each continent in a different colour. Some maps show Australia as Oceania - say both names. Misconception: children think the UK is a continent. Remind them that the UK is a country in the continent of Europe.

teach.heading: Biggest and smallest
bullets: Asia is the biggest continent.
Australia is the smallest continent.
Antarctica is covered in ice.
teach.note: Compare sizes by showing the continents as coloured shapes on a screen. Ask: which is bigger, Africa or Europe? Africa is much bigger. Link to home: many families have roots in Asia or Africa; ask children to point out where their family comes from.

teach.heading: Where are we?
bullets: The UK is in the continent of Europe.
Makkah is in Asia, in the country of Saudi Arabia.
Egypt is in the north of Africa.
teach.note: Point to each place on the map. Ask children to name a place they have visited and say which continent it is in. Makkah is a place Muslims all over the world face when they pray; this helps children connect the map with their own lives.

practice: On the world map, point to Asia, Africa and Europe as I say them.
Complete: 'The UK is in the continent of ___.'
independent: Colour in the seven continents on the world map and write their names.
Label the continent where you live and the continent where your family comes from.
Stretch: put the continents in order from biggest to smallest using a table.
exit: Which continent is the UK in?
lessons.homework: Find the seven continents on a globe or map at home and teach someone how to say them.
lessons.send: Provide a map with the continents outlined and name cards to stick on. EAL: say each continent name together twice. Stretch: ask which continents the Equator crosses.

lessons.title: The five oceans
objectives: Find the oceans on a world map
Say that most of the Earth is covered by water

keywords.def: a very large area of salt water
the biggest ocean on Earth
the ocean between Europe/Africa and the Americas
a smaller part of an ocean, often near land

starter: Which continent is the UK in?

teach.heading: Water on Earth
bullets: Most of the Earth is covered by water.
About 7 out of every 10 parts is water.
The biggest areas of water are oceans.
teach.note: Show a globe from the Pacific side so that nearly all you see is blue. Ask: is there more land or more water? Say 'about seven parts out of ten are water'. Use a picture of 10 squares with 7 coloured blue if helpful.

teach.heading: Five oceans
bullets: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
The Pacific Ocean is the biggest.
The Arctic Ocean is the smallest.
teach.note: Teach the names with a rhythm: Pa-ci-fic, At-lan-tic. Colour each ocean on the map in a different shade of blue. Ask children to point to the ocean that touches the UK: the Atlantic (and the North Sea, which is part of it).

teach.heading: Oceans and continents
bullets: Oceans lie between the continents.
The Atlantic lies between Europe and America.
The Indian Ocean is next to Africa and Asia.
teach.note: Move your finger along the coasts. Ask: if you sailed west from the UK across the Atlantic, which continent would you reach? (North America). Keep language simple and use arrows on the map.

teach.heading: Looking after the sea
bullets: Many animals live in the ocean.
Litter and plastic can harm sea animals.
We can reuse, recycle and put litter in the bin.
teach.note: Show a picture of a turtle or fish tangled in plastic. Ask children how it must feel. Connect to being kind to Allah's creation and looking after the Earth as a trust. Ask them to suggest one thing they can do at home.

practice: Point to the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean on the map.
Say: 'The Indian Ocean is next to ___.' Choose a continent.
independent: Label the five oceans on a world map.
Colour the oceans in blue and the continents in green.
Stretch: write one sentence about an animal that lives in the ocean.
exit: Is there more land or more water on Earth?
lessons.homework: Draw an ocean animal and write the name of the ocean where it lives.
lessons.send: Use pre-labelled oceans for support. EAL: rehearse ocean names with a rhythm. Stretch: ask which ocean is nearest to the child's family home country.

lessons.title: Hot and cold places: the Equator and the Poles
objectives: Find the Equator, the North Pole and the South Pole
Say that places near the Equator are hot and places near the Poles are cold
Describe one hot place and one cold place

keywords.def: an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth
the very top of the Earth, a very cold place
the very bottom of the Earth, a very cold place
a place that gets very little rain

starter: Is it hot or cold outside today in the UK?

teach.heading: The Equator
bullets: The Equator is an imaginary line.
It goes around the middle of the Earth.
It is not a real line on the ground.
teach.note: Use a globe or a ball with a string around the middle. Point to countries that the Equator crosses, such as Ecuador, Kenya and Indonesia. Misconception: some pupils think the Equator is a real line you can see. Explain that it is a line drawn on maps to help us.

teach.heading: Hot places
bullets: Places near the Equator are hot.
The sun shines strongly there all year.
The Sahara in Africa is a very hot desert.
teach.note: Show a photograph of the Sahara and of a hot rainforest. Ask: what do people wear? What do plants and animals need to survive? Explain that a desert gets very little rain but a rainforest gets lots of rain, and both can be hot.

teach.heading: Cold places
bullets: The North Pole is at the top of the Earth.
The South Pole is at the bottom.
Places near the Poles are very, very cold.
teach.note: Show Antarctica and the Arctic on the globe. Share that in Antarctica the temperature has fallen to about minus 89 degrees Celsius, the coldest ever recorded. Ask: what clothes would you need? Explain that polar bears live in the Arctic and penguins in Antarctica.

teach.heading: Where is the UK?
bullets: The UK is between the Equator and the North Pole.
The UK is not very hot or very cold.
We have mild weather with four seasons.
teach.note: Use a sorting line: hot (Equator), medium (UK), cold (Pole). Ask where the UK sits and why we need both coats and sun hats in a year. Praise children for using 'because'.

practice: Point to the Equator on the globe. Point to the North Pole.
Sort the pictures into hot places and cold places.
independent: Draw the Equator and the two Poles on a picture of the Earth.
Colour the hot places red and the cold places blue.
Stretch: write two sentences comparing a hot place and a cold place.
exit: Are places near the Equator hot or cold?
lessons.homework: Draw what you would pack for a trip to the Sahara and what you would pack for the North Pole.
lessons.send: Give a labelled globe diagram. EAL: pair words with pictures (hot/cold, near/far). Stretch: ask why it is warmer near the Equator, using the idea that the sun shines more directly.

lessons.title: Using an atlas and a compass
objectives: Use an atlas or world map to find a place
Use north, south, east and west to describe where places are

keywords.def: a book of maps
a tool that shows direction
the direction towards the North Pole
which way something is, like north or south

starter: Say Bismillah. Is the Equator hot or cold?
Which continent is the UK in?

teach.heading: What is an atlas?
bullets: An atlas is a book of maps.
It shows continents, countries and cities.
There is an index at the back to find places.
teach.note: Show an atlas or an online atlas page. Model looking up Egypt in the index and finding the page. Ask children how the index is like the contents page of a story book. Keep a copy of the world map visible throughout.

teach.heading: Four compass points
bullets: The four main directions are north, east, south and west.
North is usually at the top of a map.
Never Eat Soggy Waffles helps us remember the order.
teach.note: Draw a compass rose and label N, E, S, W going clockwise. Teach the rhyme 'Never Eat Shredded Wheat' or 'Never Eat Soggy Waffles'. Have children stand and point north (the front of the room), then east to their right. Muslims also use direction when finding the qibla: it is the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah.

teach.heading: Describing where places are
bullets: Scotland is north of England.
Wales is west of England.
France is south of the UK.
teach.note: Use a map of the UK and Europe. Ask children to complete sentences: ___ is north of ___. Watch for children confusing east and west. Point out that on a map, east is to the right.

teach.heading: Finding a place
bullets: Choose a place and find it in the index.
Turn to the page and find the place.
Say which continent and direction it is.
teach.note: Model three steps aloud (think aloud). Example: find Egypt. The index gives a page. On the map, Egypt is in the north of Africa and south-east of the UK. Give children a place card each to find on their own map.

practice: Use the compass rose to say which direction Scotland is from England.
Find Egypt on the map and say which continent it is in.
independent: Label the compass rose with N, E, S and W.
Complete five sentences using north, south, east and west about places on the UK map.
Stretch: write directions to move from the school gate to the library on a simple map.
exit: What do we call a book of maps?
Which direction is at the top of most maps?
lessons.homework: Use a map or phone compass to find north in your home and tell someone which room is in the north.
lessons.send: Provide a compass rose with the letters partly filled in. EAL: practise direction words with movement. Stretch: introduce north-east and north-west.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Towers and bridges around the world (Towers, Tunnels & Turrets)
lessons.title: Amazing towers around the world
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do people build towers so high?
objectives: To understand where some famous towers are in the world and why they were built
successCriteria: Most: find their countries on a world map
Some: say which continent each is in
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the adhan calls everyone to prayer

keywords.def: a tall, narrow building
a flat picture of all the land and sea on Earth
a very large area of land
a land with its own name and leaders
a tower of a masjid where the adhan is called

hook.text: What is the tallest building you have ever seen? How tall do you think it was?

islamicLink.text: Masjids around the world have minarets so the adhan can be heard far away. The adhan reminds us five times a day that Allah is the Greatest.

starter.a: For example: stone, brick, metal, glass, wood

teach.heading: Towers in Britain
bullets: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben), London
The White Tower, London
Castle turrets
teach.note: Find London on the UK map.

teach.heading: Towers of the world
bullets: Burj Khalifa, Dubai: tallest building
Eiffel Tower, Paris, France
Leaning Tower of Pisa, Italy
teach.note: Find each on the world map. The Burj Khalifa is 828 metres tall.

teach.heading: Minarets
bullets: A minaret is a masjid tower
The adhan is called from high up
Hassan II Mosque, Morocco, Africa
teach.note: The minaret of the Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca is one of the tallest in the world.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: It is in Paris, the capital of France.

practice.q: Which country is the Burj Khalifa in?
practice.model:
I find the tower in the table.
Burj Khalifa: Dubai.
Dubai is in the United Arab Emirates.
So: United Arab Emirates.

practice.q: Why is the adhan called from a minaret?
practice.a: So people far away can hear it

independent.q: Core: Draw a dot on the world map for three towers and label them.
independent.a: Dots in France, Italy and the United Arab Emirates (or Canada) with labels
independent.model: Teacher puts the first dot on Paris, France and labels 'Eiffel Tower'.

independent.q: Extend: Write the continent next to each tower.
independent.a: Europe, Europe, Asia (North America for the CN Tower)

independent.q: Stretch: Why might people build very tall towers?
independent.a: To look out, to call the adhan, to show skill, or for offices and homes

exit.q: A minaret is part of a:
Big question: why do people build towers so high?
exit.a: To see far, be seen, call the adhan far and wide, or fit more rooms on less land

lessons.homework: Find a tall building or tower near your home (from a window or online) and tell your family what it is for.
lessons.send: SEND: map with tower stickers. EAL: tower, country, map with pictures. Stretch: order four towers from tallest to shortest using online facts with an adult.

lessons.unit: Summer 1: My local area, maps and aerial images (Street Detectives)
lessons.title: Street detectives: features of my local area
lessons.bigQuestion: What clues does your street give about the people who live there?
objectives: To understand that a local area has human and physical features we can observe and record
successCriteria: All: sort features into human and physical
Most: record features seen from my door or window
Some: say what my street is used for
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: counting with ticks and tallies
lessons.smsc: Social: caring for the street we share with neighbours

keywords.def: the streets and places near your home
a road with houses or shops along it
something people built, like a shop
something nature made, like a stream
look carefully and notice

hook.text: If a detective looked at your street, what would they notice first?

starter.q: A castle's water ditch is a:
Name one tall tower in the world.
starter.a: For example: the Eiffel Tower or the Burj Khalifa

teach.heading: Be a street detective
bullets: Look carefully
Notice small clues
Write down what you see
teach.note: Fieldwork from the door or window only, with an adult. No going out alone.

teach.heading: Human or physical?
bullets: Human: houses, shops, roads, lamp posts
Physical: trees, grass, hills, streams
teach.note: Physical features are part of Allah's creation; human features are built by people.

teach.heading: Recording what we see
bullets: Use a tick list
One tick for each feature
Add a photo or quick sketch
teach.note: Model with a photo of a street: 4 houses, 2 trees, 1 post box.

steps: Write H or P beside each

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: People built the lamp post; streams and hills are natural.

practice.model:
Did people build grass?
No, it grows by itself.
So it is physical.

practice.q: Is a bus stop human or physical?
Name a human feature on your street.
practice.a: For example: houses, a shop, a road

independent.q: Core: From your door or window, with an adult, tick each feature you can see and write H or P beside it.
independent.a: A completed tick list from the pupil's own street, each marked H or P
independent.model: Teacher completes the first row with the class photo.

independent.q: Extend: What is your street mostly used for: homes, shops or both?
independent.a: For example: mostly homes, with one shop

independent.q: Stretch: Name one feature you would like to add to your street and why.
independent.a: For example: a bench, so older people can rest

exit.q: Big question: what clues does your street give?
exit.a: For example: lots of houses show people live there; a shop shows people buy things

lessons.homework: Take two photos of your street (no people) with an adult: one human feature and one physical feature.
lessons.send: SEND: picture tick list. EAL: feature word cards with photos. Stretch: count which kind of feature you saw more of.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 2 curriculum map and science, history and geography long-term plans 2023-24; TGA Year 2 pack, Topic, Summer 1 Street Detectives (companion: How Do Germs Spread?) (Cornerstones Maestro: CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Clipboard or book and pencil; a door or window at home (fieldwork from home with an adult; no trips)

lessons.unit: Summer 1: My local area, maps and aerial images (Street Detectives)
lessons.title: A map of my street with a key and compass
lessons.bigQuestion: How could a visitor find your front door using only a map?
objectives: To understand how maps use symbols, a key and compass directions
successCriteria: All: draw simple symbols for features
Most: make a key for my map
Some: use north, east, south and west
lessons.smsc: Social: helping visitors find their way

keywords.def: a drawing of a place from above
a small picture that stands for something
a box that tells you what each symbol means
a tool that shows north, east, south and west
the direction at the top of most maps

hook.text: Why do maps use little pictures instead of photos?

starter.q: Living memory is the past that:
Name one thing that has changed since your grandparents were young.
starter.a: For example: mobile phones or more cars

teach.heading: Maps are from above
bullets: Like a bird looking down
Houses look like squares
Roads look like long strips
teach.note: Hold a cup above the camera, then look down at it: a circle.

teach.heading: Symbols and a key
bullets: A symbol is a small picture
The key says what it means
Keep symbols simple
teach.note: Example: a green circle for a tree, a red square for a post box.

teach.heading: Compass directions
bullets: North at the top
East to the right
South at the bottom
West to the left
teach.note: Spoken memory chant (no music): Never Eat Shredded Wheat, going round clockwise.

teach.heading: Draw a street map
bullets: Draw the road first
Add your house
Add symbols and a key
Draw an arrow for north
teach.note: Model a whole street map on the whiteboard.

steps: Draw the road as two lines
Add a green circle for each tree
model.answer: A street map with symbols, a key and north

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: On most maps, north is at the:
check.why: Maps usually have north at the top; south is at the bottom.

practice.q: What tells you what the symbols mean?
practice.model:
I see a red square.
I do not know what it is.
I look in the key.
It says post box.

independent.q: Core: Draw a map of your street with at least four symbols, a key and an arrow showing north.
independent.a: A street map with 4 or more symbols, a matching key and a north arrow
independent.model: Teacher shows the model map and points to the key.

independent.q: Extend: Write one sentence using a compass direction, e.g. 'The tree is east of my house.'
independent.a: A correct sentence using north, east, south or west

independent.q: Stretch: Give directions from your house to the post box.
independent.a: For example: go east along the road, the post box is on the left

exit.q: Big question: how could a visitor find your door?
exit.a: Follow the map: use the road, the symbols and the key, and north

lessons.homework: Ask an adult which way is north at home (a compass app helps) and add it to your map.
lessons.send: SEND: a street outline to add symbols to. EAL: N, E, S, W cards. Stretch: add a scale line saying 'about 10 steps'.

Phone compass app with an adult (optional)

lessons.unit: Summer 1: My local area, maps and aerial images (Street Detectives)
lessons.title: Aerial and satellite views of a street; review quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: What can a satellite see that you cannot see from your front door?
objectives: To understand how aerial and satellite images show a street from above and how they compare with maps
successCriteria: All: find features on an aerial image
Most: match an aerial image to a map
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: satellites and space from Year 1
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: seeing our homes from above as part of Allah's wide earth

keywords.def: seen from high in the air
a machine in space that circles the Earth
a picture or photo
what you can see from one place
look back at what we learned

hook.text: If you could float above your house, what would your roof look like?

starter.q: On a map, a symbol is explained by the:

teach.heading: From the air
bullets: Aerial photos: from planes and drones
Satellite images: from space
We see roofs, roads and trees
teach.note: Recap Year 1: Earth from space.

teach.heading: Find the clues
bullets: Roads are grey lines
Trees are green blobs
Roofs are shapes in rows
teach.note: With an adult, online maps can show your street from above.

model.problem: Find the park on the image
steps: Look for a big green patch
model.answer: The green patch is the park

teach.heading: Image or map?
bullets: The image shows real colours
The map uses symbols
Both are from above
teach.note: Show a satellite image and a map of the same street side by side.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Vote in the Teams poll
teach.note: Share the results.

options: A machine circling Earth in space
check.why: Satellites go round the Earth in space and take pictures; planes fly much lower.

practice.q: On an aerial photo, what colour are trees?
practice.model:
Trees have leaves.
From above we see the tops of the leaves.
They look like green blobs.

practice.q: Which has a key: a map or a satellite image?

independent.q: Core: Review quiz in the portal: 8 questions on human and physical features, symbols, keys, compass points, then and now, germs and handwashing.
independent.a: Answers on the quiz key; aim for 6 or more
independent.model: Teacher reads question 1 and shows how to choose an answer.

independent.q: Extend: On the aerial image sheet, circle a road, a tree and a roof.
Stretch: Write one thing a satellite image shows that a map does not.

exit.q: Big question: what can a satellite see that you cannot?
exit.a: The whole street from above: roofs, gardens and roads together

lessons.homework: With an adult, find your street on an online map and switch to the satellite view. Spot your roof.
lessons.send: SEND: quiz read aloud; picture options. EAL: aerial, satellite, map with pictures. Stretch: compare a satellite image of your street with your own map.
